name: The General Will
statement: Legitimate law expresses the general will, the community's shared aim at the common good, not just the sum of private interests.
statementAccent: the community's shared aim at the common good
meaning: The general will is a central concept in the political philosophy of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, developed most fully in his 1762 book The Social Contract, referring to the collective will of the citizen body taken as a whole, directed at the common good of the community. Rousseau distinguished the general will, which aims at the shared interest of all, from what he called the will of all, which is merely the sum of individual private and particular interests. For Rousseau, a state is legitimate only if it is guided by the general will, and law and sovereign authority are the expression of that will; sovereignty belongs inalienably to the people, so legitimate government rests on popular sovereignty. Because in obeying a law that expresses the general will each citizen is in a sense obeying their own deeper will, Rousseau argued that submission to the general will is compatible with freedom, indeed a form of obeying oneself. From this he drew his most controversial claim, that anyone who refuses to obey the general will may be forced to do so by the whole community, which, he wrote, means that they will be forced to be free. The general will became foundational to democratic theory and popular sovereignty, and also a lasting subject of debate.
mechanism: The general will operates as the standard of legitimacy for law and government in Rousseau's theory. When people form a political community through the social contract, they do not surrender their freedom to a ruler but unite to form a collective body whose will, when it aims at the common good shared by all citizens, is the general will. This is different in kind from the will of all, the mere aggregate of individual desires each pursuing private advantage; the general will emerges when citizens set aside their particular interests and consider what is good for the community as a whole. Legitimate law is precisely law that expresses the general will, and the sovereign, which for Rousseau is the assembled people, cannot alienate or be represented in this will. Because each citizen is both a member of the sovereign that makes the law and a subject bound by it, obeying the general will is understood as obeying a will that is genuinely one's own as a citizen, so it preserves rather than destroys freedom. Rousseau's difficult conclusion follows: if a person lets their private will diverge from the general will and refuses to obey the law, the community may compel them, and in doing so it forces them to be free, aligning them with their own higher civic will. How the general will is actually to be known and identified, however, Rousseau leaves genuinely unclear.

variants.name: Popular sovereignty
variants.text: The doctrine, grounded in the general will, that legitimate authority rests with the sovereign people rather than a ruler.

variants.name: The authoritarian critique
variants.text: The charge, from critics like Talmon and Constant, that forced to be free opens the way to coercion in the name of the collective.

whyItMatters: The general will is one of the most influential and provocative ideas in modern political philosophy, giving powerful expression to the principle of popular sovereignty, the doctrine that legitimate political authority resides in the people as a whole rather than in a monarch or ruling class. By arguing that legitimate law is the expression of a collective will aimed at the common good, and that citizens who make the law are free in obeying it, Rousseau provided a philosophical foundation for democratic self-government and republicanism that has shaped political thought ever since. His ideas directly influenced the French Revolution, and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man defined law as the expression of the general will. The concept also frames enduring debates about the relationship between the individual and the collective, between private interest and the common good, and about how a community can act as a genuine unity. At the same time, its ambiguity and its most striking implication, that people might be forced to be free, made it a focus of warnings about the dangers of collective coercion. As the idea that legitimate law expresses the shared will of a sovereign people, the general will is a cornerstone of democratic theory.

working.text: have citizens unite through the social contract into a political community with a shared will.
let the general will emerge as they set aside private interest to will what is good for all, unlike the mere will of all.
treat legitimate law as the expression of the general will, so that in obeying it citizens obey their own civic will.

limits: The general will is a powerful but genuinely ambiguous concept, and its difficulties are central to its interpretation. Commentators disagree over what the general will actually is, with a democratic reading treating it as what citizens decide together in assembly and a more transcendent reading treating it as the common interest in abstraction from what anyone actually wants, so there is a real epistemic problem of how the general will is to be known. Rousseau's argument that outvoted citizens are still obeying their own will is widely found unpersuasive, exposing the tension between individual and collective. Most seriously, the claim that a person may be forced to be free has been criticized as opening the door to authoritarianism, with critics such as Jacob Talmon and Benjamin Constant charging Rousseau with authoritarianism, though many scholars hold that he was concerned with civil liberty and autonomy rather than with unchecked government power. So the general will robustly expresses popular sovereignty and the common good, understood as an ambiguous concept whose relation to individual freedom and whose forced to be free clause are deeply contested.
misreadings: The general will is not simply majority opinion or the sum of what individuals want; that is the will of all, whereas the general will aims at the common good of the community. Rousseau's phrase forced to be free is not straightforwardly a licence for tyranny in his own intent, though critics warn it can become one, so its meaning is contested rather than plainly authoritarian. And the general will is not easy to identify, since how it is known is genuinely unclear, so treating it as mere majority will, as openly endorsing coercion, or as transparently knowable, misreads an ambiguous and much-debated concept of popular sovereignty.
origin: A central concept in the political philosophy of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, developed in his 1762 book The Social Contract, holding that legitimate law expresses the general will aimed at the common good.
